value.overview: The Ring-necked/Green Pheasant is an eBird composite or slash taxon used when closely related pheasant forms are not separated confidently. Field recognition often comes from male pheasant pattern, long tail, glossy green head, red face skin, pale neck ring when present, and warm copper body; females are mottled brown and much more cryptic. In the U.S. source data, it appeared in 22 state or DC summaries, including CA, CO, IA, ID, IL, IN, KS, MI, MN, MO, MT, ND, NE, NM, and 8 more. It is most associated with Wetlands:  Generalist and Wetlands:  Generalist, and local season should be checked before trip planning.
value.classification: The Ring-necked/Green Pheasant belongs to the family Pheasants, Grouse, and Allies in the order Galliformes. This is the practical birding classification used for the BirdIntel profile cache.
value.identification: Look for male pheasant pattern, long tail, glossy green head, red face skin, pale neck ring when present, and warm copper body; females are mottled brown and much more cryptic. Also use size, posture, flight style, voice, behavior, habitat, and season. Plumage can vary by sex, age, molt, and light, so the safest identification comes from combining several field marks rather than relying on one color or feature.

value.migrationStatus: In the United States, it can be resident in suitable parts of its range, although local movement may occur with food, weather, or water conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding is ground based, with nests hidden in grass, sagebrush, agricultural edges, or other dense cover. Chicks are precocial and feed themselves soon after hatching, while adults rely on cover for protection. Local success depends heavily on intact Wetlands:  Generalist and Wetlands:  Generalist.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mostly on seeds, leaves, shoots, berries, cultivated grain, and insects. Feeding is mainly on the ground, often in grassland, shrubland, farm edges, or open woodland.
value.behavior: It spends much time walking in cover and usually flushes with loud wingbeats when disturbed. Males can be conspicuous during display, while females remain more hidden around nesting cover.
